Measuring and comparing configurations

Source: vignettes/evaluate.Rmd
evaluate.Rmd

Every choice in a pipeline (the recipe, the model, the prompt, the reasoning effort) changes the answers, and one run on one document cannot say by how much. A model asked the same question five times can answer it five ways, and ten questions about one report share that report’s quirks, so they are closer to one observation than to ten. gr_compare() shows what each recipe does to one document and is descriptive only. The functions in this guide answer the question that follows it: on a labelled set of questions, is configuration A more accurate than B, by how much, at what cost, and how sure can you be?

The guide follows the order of the work: a reference set and its splits, the arms to compare and the rule that scores them, a benchmark held to one spending limit, the report and how to read it, planning the size of a comparison before running it, judges, baselines that use no model, drift, and the signals the package records about its own work. The statistics functions underneath come last. Measuring a screener against people, several reviewers and agreement between extraction tables are part of a review and are in vignette("review").

Setting up

Everything below runs offline. gr_mock_client() stands in for the model, and embedder = "lexical" keeps retrieval free and deterministic. Two mock model ids get prices, so the benchmarks below have a cost to compare: mock-small at $0.20 and $0.80 per million input and output tokens, and mock-large at ten times that.

library(harnessr)
old <- gr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")

gr_register_model("mock-small", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 0.2, output_usd = 0.8)
gr_register_model("mock-large", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 2, output_usd = 8)

References and splits

A reference is the labelled set every configuration is scored on. Each item has a payload (what the configuration is given), a label (what counts as right), a cluster and a split. The cluster is the unit whose items share errors, usually the document: eight questions about one report are not eight independent observations, and every interval in this guide is computed with that in mind. hr_reference() builds one from any items; gr_qa_reference() builds one of questions about documents, with each question’s acceptable answers:

reports <- c(
  north = "The northern region. Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024. The plant in Leeds made 12,400 units.",
  south = "The southern region. Revenue was 51.8 million dollars in fiscal 2025. Staff numbered 310 at year end.",
  east  = "The eastern region. Revenue was 38.9 million dollars in fiscal 2024. The chair is Ana Ruiz.",
  west  = "The western region. Revenue was 29.4 million dollars in fiscal 2023. Exports rose 7 percent.")

qa <- gr_qa_reference(
  questions = c(n_rev = "What was revenue?", n_units = "How many units did Leeds make?",
                s_rev = "What was revenue?", s_staff = "How many staff were there?",
                e_rev = "What was revenue?", e_ceo = "Who is the chief executive?",
                w_rev = "What was revenue?", w_exp = "By how much did exports rise?"),
  documents = rep(unname(reports), each = 2),
  answers = list("45.2 million", c("12,400", "12400"), "51.8 million", "310",
                 "38.9 million", NA, "29.4 million", "7 percent"),
  unanswerable = "e_ceo",
  cluster = rep(names(reports), each = 2),
  split = "test")
qa
#> <hr_reference> 8 item(s) in 4 cluster(s)
#>   splits: test 8 
#>   hash: d64da50d3779

The eastern report names a chair and no chief executive, so e_ceo is marked unanswerable: its label is the not-found answer, and a reader is right on it only when it says the document does not hold the answer. The flag goes into the label alone; the payload a configuration is given holds the question and the document, so it cannot tell which questions have no answer. A reference without such items never tests whether a reader can tell that an answer is missing. An item with neither an answer nor the unanswerable flag has no label, and every run on it is scored NA, so it never counts for or against an arm.

Once a benchmark starts scoring a reference, the reference is locked: hr_reference_add() then refuses to add items to it, or to any copy of it, with an error of class hr_reference_locked, so no item can be added after the results are seen. The reference also carries a SHA-256 hash of its content, which the benchmark checks.

Splits keep tuning apart from evidence. dev is for tuning prompts, settings and margins, and its scores are never reported. exploratory holds early experiments, calibration is for fitting signal thresholds (below), test is what reported comparisons are scored on, and final, if used, is held back and run once per release. hr_assign_splits() assigns whole clusters, so no document has questions on both sides of a tuning and a scoring split:

questions <- data.frame(
  item_id  = sprintf("q%03d", 1:120),
  document = rep(sprintf("report%02d.pdf", 1:30), each = 4),
  question = rep(c("What was revenue?", "Who audited the accounts?",
                   "How many staff were there?", "When did the year end?"), 30))
sp <- hr_assign_splits(questions, seed = 2026)
sp
#> <hr_splits> 120 item(s) in 30 cluster(s), method stable, seed 2026
#> 
#>        split target clusters items cluster_share item_share
#>          dev    0.1        4    16         0.133      0.133
#>  exploratory    0.1        3    12         0.100      0.100
#>  calibration    0.3       10    40         0.333      0.333
#>         test    0.5       13    52         0.433      0.433

The default shares are 10% dev, 10% exploratory, 30% calibration and 50% test. Each cluster’s place comes from the SHA-256 digest of the seed and its id, so row order and the session’s random state do not change it, and with the default method = "stable" adding or dropping a document never moves another. The price is that the shares are met only on average: 13 of these 30 documents went to test, not 15. method = "balanced" gives each split its share of whole clusters, at the cost that a document added later can shift others across a boundary, so draw it once and store it:

hr_assign_splits(questions, seed = 2026, method = "balanced")$counts[, c("split", "clusters", "items")]
#>         split clusters items
#> 1         dev        3    12
#> 2 exploratory        3    12
#> 3 calibration        9    36
#> 4        test       15    60

A split given a share that receives no cluster warns with class hr_empty_split, which happens with very few documents.

Label sheets

Labels come from people. gr_label_sheet() writes a CSV with one row per item, the columns a person needs to judge it and empty columns for their decisions, with an instructions file beside it. It writes five kinds: "qa", "screening", "extraction", "calibration" and "judge". A blind sheet, the default, copies only those columns, so a model’s answer in items stays out of it:

to_label <- head(sp$items, 3)
to_label$model_answer <- c("45.2 million", "Not stated", "310")

path <- file.path(tempdir(), "qa-labels.csv")
sheet <- gr_label_sheet("qa", to_label, path = path)
names(sheet)
#> [1] "item_id"    "document"   "question"   "answerable" "answer"    
#> [6] "quote"      "note"

The person fills answerable, answer and quote. gr_read_labels() reads the sheet back, checks every value and id, and joins the items’ other columns back by item_id, renaming one that clashes with a decision column (the model’s answer here would come back as model_answer):

filled <- read.csv(path, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
filled$answerable <- c("yes", "no", "yes")
filled$answer <- c("45.2 million dollars", NA, "310")
write.csv(filled, path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")

gr_read_labels(path, "qa", items = to_label)[, c("item_id", "answerable", "answer",
                                                  "split", "model_answer")]
#>   item_id answerable               answer split model_answer
#> 1    q001       TRUE 45.2 million dollars   dev 45.2 million
#> 2    q002      FALSE                 <NA>   dev   Not stated
#> 3    q003       TRUE                  310   dev          310

A value it cannot read stops it with an error of class gr_bad_labels that names the sheet, the row as a spreadsheet counts it and the item, for every bad value at once:

filled$answer[2] <- "Smith & Co"
write.csv(filled, path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
tryCatch(gr_read_labels(path, "qa", items = to_label),
         gr_bad_labels = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e)))
#> 1 value(s) in the qa sheet cannot be read:
#> qa-labels.csv row 3 (item 'q002'): `answerable` is no but `answer` is filled; clear one of them.

With reviewers = k each person gets a sheet of their own, so no one sees another’s decisions. ?gr_label_sheet gives the number of items each kind of set needs for the package’s own evaluation: for question answering, about 480 questions over 88 documents.

Arms and scorers

An arm is one configuration to compare: a function of an item and a context that returns the arm’s output for that item. ctx carries the benchmark’s client, a trace of this run alone, the governor the run is held to and the run’s draw_index; ctx$call() is gr_call() with the client, the trace and the draw index filled in. Every request an arm makes has to go through that trace, since it is how the benchmark counts the run’s tokens and dollars and holds it to the limit:

ask <- function(name, model) {
  hr_arm(name, function(item, ctx) {
    ctx$call(paste("Item", item), model = ctx$params$model)$text
  }, params = list(model = model))
}
ask("large", "mock-large")
#> <hr_arm large> version 0.0.1
#>   params: model = mock-large 
#>   hash: dc2928258ae6

The arm records a SHA-256 hash of its name, code, settings and version. The code is hashed as text with the values it names from the environment it was made in, the workspace included: an arm written at top level that reads a global prompt gets a new hash when the prompt changes. The same arm has the same hash in every session and after saveRDS(), and an arm edited after it was built is refused rather than run under its old name. Change version when the arm’s behaviour changes.

gr_arm() wraps a reading recipe as an arm, and gr_arms() builds one per recipe. Each run reads the item’s document with answer_document(), or with gr_read() when the document is already chunked, and returns the gr_answer. settings takes what answer_document() takes in ...; here they make the same recipe two arms on two models:

arms <- list(gr_arm("fast", settings = list(model = "mock-small"), name = "small"),
             gr_arm("fast", settings = list(model = "mock-large"), name = "large"))

A gr_arm()’s version is the package version, since readers and prompts change between releases. Every request of a run, segmenter and reader requests included, carries the run’s draw index. A reader that finds the run’s limits leave it too little room to start returns a partial not-found answer noting the limit, which is scored as a budget stop rather than an error.

A scorer turns an output and a label into correct, an outcome (what it compared) and a failure_kind saying why a wrong output was wrong: "parse_failure", "refusal", "not_in_document", "wrong", "budget_stop" or "error". hr_scorer_exact(), the default, compares text after folding case and white space. gr_scorer_answer() is the one for reading recipes: an answer is right when it contains any acceptable answer, after folding case, white space and thousands separators, with numbers matched whole ("12" is not found in ".12" or "-12", but is found in "12-15", and "45.2" in "45.2m"):

s <- gr_scorer_answer()
item <- list(question = "How many units?", document = gr_example())
s$fn(item, "Leeds made 12,400 units.", "12400")$correct
#> [1] TRUE
s$fn(item, "Leeds made 112,400 units.", "12400")$correct
#> [1] FALSE
s$fn(item, "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", "12400")$failure_kind
#> [1] "wrong"

On an unanswerable item it is right when is_not_found() is TRUE and no limit or refusal stopped the run, since a reader that ran out of budget did not look. hr_scorer() makes a scorer of your own from a function of (item, output, label); its help has one that accepts a number within 1% of the label.

Running a benchmark

hr_benchmark() runs every arm on every item of the chosen splits runs times, scores each output, and returns one row per cluster, item, arm and run. The stand-in model below knows each report’s facts. Asked as mock-small it loses its way on 30% of requests; as mock-large it does not:

facts <- list(
  northern = c(revenue = "Revenue was 45.2 million dollars.", units = "Leeds made 12,400 units."),
  southern = c(revenue = "Revenue was 51.8 million dollars.", staff = "There were 310 staff."),
  eastern  = c(revenue = "Revenue was 38.9 million dollars."),
  western  = c(revenue = "Revenue was 29.4 million dollars.", exports = "Exports rose 7 percent."))

cl <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  seen <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), ""), collapse = " ")
  region <- regmatches(seen, regexpr("(northern|southern|eastern|western)", seen))
  asked <- sub(".*Question", "", seen)
  topic <- c("revenue", "units", "staff", "exports")
  hit <- topic[vapply(topic, grepl, logical(1), x = asked, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
  reply <- facts[[region]][hit]
  if (is.na(reply)) return("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT")
  if (identical(params$model, "mock-small") && runif(1) < 0.3) return("The report is unclear.")
  reply
})

bench <- hr_benchmark(arms, qa, runs = 5, client = cl, scorer = gr_scorer_answer())
bench
#> <hr_bench> 2 arm(s) x 8 item(s) in 4 cluster(s) x 5 run(s); split test; scorer answer_contains
#>  arm   accuracy runs wrong failed budget_stop usd   
#>  small 0.750    40   10    0      0           0.0013
#>  large 1.000    40    0    0      0           0.0132
#>   Descriptive only: accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over labelled items, with no interval.
head(bench[, c("item", "arm", "run", "correct", "failure_kind", "usd", "draw_index")])
#>    item   arm run correct failure_kind      usd draw_index
#> 1 n_rev small   1   FALSE        wrong 3.10e-05          1
#> 2 n_rev small   2    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-05          2
#> 3 n_rev small   3    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-05          3
#> 4 n_rev small   4    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-05          4
#> 5 n_rev small   5   FALSE        wrong 3.10e-05          5
#> 6 n_rev large   1    TRUE         <NA> 3.42e-04          1

The printed accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over items, and is descriptive: no interval. The arms run under a private random stream started from seed (1 by default), which is why the mock’s runif() gives the same draws every time this guide is built, and the caller’s random state is left as it was. Rows on the dev split are marked reportable = FALSE and printed apart. Five runs is the default and the expected minimum; fewer warns with class hr_few_runs, because with fewer the spread from run to run cannot be told from the difference between arms.

One limit for the whole benchmark

The benchmark is one run under one hr_governor(). Each run’s trace is held to the governor’s limits less what the runs before it used, so the limit you set is the most the whole comparison can spend. With governor = NULL the limits come from gr_options(), whose default of 400 calls is easy to exceed: two arms on 300 items for 5 runs is 3000 calls. A run stopped by a refused request is recorded as a "budget_stop", counted wrong, and the runs after it are still started, so every row exists and the refusals are visible:

capitals <- hr_reference(items = list(q1 = "France", q2 = "Peru", q3 = "Chad", q4 = "Fiji"),
                         labels = c("Paris", "Lima", "N'Djamena", "Suva"),
                         cluster = c("a", "a", "b", "b"), split = "test")
atlas <- c(France = "Paris", Peru = "Lima", Chad = "N'Djamena", Fiji = "Suva")
geo <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) atlas[[sub("Capital of ", "", messages[[1]]$content)]])
capital <- hr_arm("capital", function(item, ctx) ctx$call(paste0("Capital of ", item))$text)

short <- hr_benchmark(capital, capitals, runs = 5, client = geo,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 6))
table(short$failure_kind, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> budget_stop        <NA> 
#>          14           6

The first six runs were answered, and the other fourteen were refused before anything was sent.

Repeated runs must be repeated draws

Run r is given ctx$draw_index = r, and ctx$call() passes it on, so under a gr_cache() each run is its own cache entry and under a gr_replay_client() its own recorded draw. The recorded draw also names the arm, so a replay answers each arm with its own replies, whether it replays every arm or a few, in any order. Five runs answered from one stored reply would agree perfectly and measure nothing, so an arm whose runs come back as copies is refused with an error of class hr_duplicate_draw. An arm that calls gr_call() without the draw index is one:

cache <- gr_cache()
cached <- gr_cache_client(geo, cache)
invisible(hr_benchmark(capital, capitals, runs = 5, client = cached))

no_draw <- hr_arm("no_draw", function(item, ctx) {
  gr_call(ctx$client, paste0("Capital of ", item), trace = ctx$trace)$text
})
tryCatch(hr_benchmark(no_draw, capitals, runs = 5, client = cached),
         hr_duplicate_draw = function(e) class(e)[1])
#> [1] "hr_duplicate_draw"

A cache is still worth having: running the capital benchmark again under the same cache sends no request and costs nothing, each run answered from its own entry. A gr_mock_client() keeps no cache, so under it the no_draw arm is not refused; under a cache it is.

Reading the report

hr_report() turns the reportable rows into accuracy per arm with intervals that keep clusters together, paired differences, stability, reliability, cost and failures. B is the number of cluster bootstrap resamples, 2000 by default; this guide uses fewer so it builds quickly.

rpt <- hr_report(bench, B = 200)
rpt
#> <hr_bench_report> 2 arm(s), 8 item(s) in 4 cluster(s), 5 run(s)
#> Intervals: cluster-robust t on the logit scale, C - 1 df at 95% (8 items in 4 clusters fall short of 300 items and 30 clusters).
#> 
#> Accuracy (arms in benchmark order, not ranked):
#>  arm   accuracy interval       rank_interval
#>  small 0.750    [0.648, 0.830] 2-2          
#>  large 1.000    [0.561, 1.000] 1-1          
#> 
#> Paired differences (first minus second):
#>  contrast      difference interval         simultaneous    
#>  small - large -0.250     [-0.342, -0.158] [-0.342, -0.158]
#> 
#> Stability across runs:
#>  arm   flip_rate TARa  run_sd
#>  small 0.750     0.250 0.153 
#>  large 0.000     1.000 0.000 
#> 
#> Reliability:
#>  arm   pass^1 pass^3 pass^5
#>  small 0.750  0.425  0.250 
#>  large 1.000  1.000  1.000 
#> 
#> Cost:
#>  arm   usd_per_item usd_per_correct interval               tokens_per_item
#>  small 3.24e-05     4.32e-05        [3.946e-05, 4.733e-05] 127.9          
#>  large 0.000331     0.000331        [0.0003192, 0.0003405] 128.8          
#>  estimated       on_frontier frontier_share
#>  100.000% (flag) yes         1.000         
#>  100.000% (flag) yes         1.000         
#> 
#> Failures (all counted wrong):
#>  arm   wrong without_parse_refusal
#>  small 10    0.750                
#>  large  0    1.000                
#> 
#> Variance on the probability scale: within-item runs 0.075, between items 0.019, within share 0.800.
#> Note: More than 5% of the cost of small, large rests on estimated token counts; read its cost as approximate. 
#> Note: Run-to-run variance is 80% of the total, above 10%: use runs = 10. 
#> Note: Cost, pass^k, frontier share and rank intervals come from the cluster bootstrap, which can undercover below 300 items or 30 clusters; read them as rough. 
#> Note: Accuracy of large is 0, 1 or the same in every cluster, where the t interval is not defined; its interval is Korn and Graubard's, one-sided from 0 or 1 at those bounds. 
#> Note: The frontier share (how often an arm is on the cost-accuracy frontier over resamples) is an extension, not a published standard.

Which interval is used depends on the size of the benchmark, and the second line of the print says which and why. With at least 300 items and at least 30 clusters, method = "auto" uses a studentised cluster bootstrap: each resample draws whole clusters with all their items, runs and arms. Below either threshold, as here, it uses a cluster-robust t interval on the logit scale, with t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom for C clusters. Where neither is defined, because accuracy is 0 or 1 or the same in every cluster, the arm gets Korn and Graubard’s interval, one-sided from that bound; that is why large reads [0.561, 1.000] with four clusters behind it, and a note says so. No interval treats items or runs as independent trials. method = "exact" (Clopper-Pearson on the effective number of items) and method = "bayes" (a beta-binomial model with a cluster random effect) are there on request.

These defaults were chosen by simulation. In dev/sim-coverage.R (2000 replicates) the studentised bootstrap covered 95.5% and 95.0% with 386 items in 40 clusters, where the BCa bootstrap it replaced covered 93.5%, and the cluster-robust t interval covered 95.7% and 95.8% with 50 items in 10 clusters. The workflow validation.yaml reruns that simulation, and the one behind hr_mdd(), every night.

Paired differences are taken item by item, so each one compares the arms on the same question, with a cluster-robust t interval at every size and simultaneous intervals over all pairs beside it. Arms are listed in benchmark order, not ranked; the rank interval is how much the order could change over resamples, and small and large here are ranked 2 and 1 in every one.

The stability rows describe each arm against itself. The flip rate is the share of items whose correctness changed between runs, TARa the share whose scored output was the same on every run, and run_sd the spread of whole-run accuracy. small flips on 75% of its items, which an accuracy of 0.750 alone would hide. Reliability is pass^k, the chance that k runs drawn from an item’s runs are all right, estimated without bias: an arm right 75% of the time is right on all five runs of an item only 25% of the time here.

Cost is in dollars and tokens per item and per correct item, since a cheap arm that is often wrong can cost more per right answer than it looks. An arm whose dollars rest on estimated token counts for more than 5% of its spend is flagged; the mock reports no token counts, so both are flagged here. The frontier is the set of arms no other arm beats on both dollars per item and accuracy, with each arm’s share of resamples on it. Failures are counted by kind, every one counted wrong, with accuracy recomputed without parse failures and refusals beside it. The variance line splits the spread into within-item (run to run) and between-item parts; when runs account for more than 10% of it, as here at 80%, the report says to use 10 runs.

Below 5 runs the report is descriptive only, with point estimates and no intervals. An item scored on some runs and not others is refused. Everything is in the returned list (rpt$accuracy, rpt$contrasts, rpt$pass_k, rpt$cost, rpt$frontier, rpt$failures, rpt$variance, rpt$notes), and as_json() writes it out.

Planning the size, and non-inferiority

Often the question is whether a cheaper arm is worse than the one in use by more than a margin you can live with. That is a non-inferiority test. Whether a benchmark can answer it depends on its size, which is worth knowing before anyone labels 500 questions.

hr_mdd() gives the smallest paired difference a clustered design can detect. It needs the number of items and clusters, the intra-cluster correlation of the paired item difference (ICC_D, taken from a pilot on the dev split) and the share of items on which the arms disagree (p_disc). For 480 questions over 80 documents:

hr_mdd(480, n_clusters = 80, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2)
#> <hr_mdd> 8.2 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.025
#>   480 items in 80 clusters (m = 6, 6 after cv 0), ICC_D 0.2: DE 2, n_eff 240
#>   p_disc 0.2
hr_mdd(480, n_clusters = 80, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2, n_contrasts = 9)
#> <hr_mdd> 10.7 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.002778 (0.025 / 9 contrasts, Holm worst case)
#>   480 items in 80 clusters (m = 6, 6 after cv 0), ICC_D 0.2: DE 2, n_eff 240
#>   p_disc 0.2

Questions in one document count for less than independent ones: the design effect DE = 1 + (m - 1) x ICC_D is 2 here, so 480 questions carry the information of 240. With nine confirmatory contrasts, Holm’s first step tests at 0.025 / 9, and the detectable difference grows from 8.2 to 10.7 points. hr_n_needed() turns it round, giving the items needed for a margin:

hr_n_needed(0.08, m = 6, icc = 0.2, p_disc = 0.2, n_contrasts = 9)
#> <hr_n_needed> 8.0 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.002778 (0.025 / 9 contrasts, Holm worst case)
#>   n_eff 419 effective items; DE 2, so 840 items in 140 clusters of 6

Both use t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom, the ones the report tests with. In the power simulation dev/sim-power.R the formula’s MDD was within 0.25 points of the simulated one; with normal quantiles it was up to 0.41 points below it at 80 clusters, which is why t quantiles are used.

hr_contrast() states a contrast (the new arm, the reference arm, the margin and whether the new arm must also be cheaper) and hr_register_contrasts() fixes the contrasts against the reference before anything scores it. The help suggests a margin of min(0.5 x M1, the loss you would accept in practice), with M1 the reference arm’s advantage over a minimal baseline in a pilot. A confirmatory margin below the design’s MDD after Holm is refused with class hr_margin_below_mdd, since it claims more than the items can show; confirmatory = FALSE registers it as exploratory instead. A reference a benchmark has already begun to score is refused with class hr_registration_after_scoring.

n <- 300
ids <- sprintf("q%03d", 1:n)
docs <- rep(sprintf("doc%02d", 1:50), each = 6)
plan <- hr_reference(ids, labels = rep("yes", n), cluster = docs, split = "test")

design <- hr_mdd(n, n_clusters = 50, icc = 0.1, p_disc = 0.15)
reg <- hr_register_contrasts(plan, hr_contrast("small", "large", margin = 0.10), design)
reg
#> <hr_contrast_registration> 1 contrast(s), 1 confirmatory; registered 2026-11-10T01:54:42.320Z
#>  contrast       label        margin mdd cost_test
#>  small vs large confirmatory 10.0   7.8 yes      
#>   Margins and MDD in points; reference d453122a93af; hash 79bccfe26832

Here the stand-in model finds each item easier or harder by document and by item, and mock-small is a little worse on every one. The governor allows the 3000 calls the benchmark needs:

set.seed(11)
ease <- setNames(rnorm(50, 2, 1)[as.integer(factor(docs))] + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5), ids)
grader <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shift <- if (identical(params$model, "mock-small")) -0.3 else 0
  item <- sub("Item ", "", messages[[1]]$content)
  if (runif(1) < plogis(ease[[item]] + shift)) "yes" else "no"
})

trial <- hr_benchmark(list(ask("large", "mock-large"), ask("small", "mock-small")),
                      plan, runs = 5, client = grader,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 4000, max_cost_usd = 1))
ni <- hr_report(trial, B = 500, registration = reg)
ni$method_reason
#> [1] "300 items in 50 clusters reach 300 items and 30 clusters"
ni$ni[, c("new", "reference", "margin", "estimate", "lower", "cost_upper",
          "verdict", "mdd_design", "mdd_achieved")]
#>     new reference margin    estimate       lower cost_upper verdict mdd_design
#> 1 small     large    0.1 -0.05266667 -0.08118863  -4.32e-05    TRUE 0.07828581
#>   mdd_achieved
#> 1   0.04057211

With 300 items in 50 clusters the report switches to the studentised bootstrap. A contrast holds only if the one-sided lower bound of the accuracy difference is above -margin and, with the cost test, the upper bound of the paired cost difference is below 0. Here small is 5.3 points less accurate than large, its lower bound is -8.1 points, inside the margin of 10, and its cost bound is below 0, so the verdict is TRUE. The accuracy bound is the cluster-robust t bound of the paired differences, so at one-sided 0.025 it is the lower end of the printed 95% contrast interval. Confirmatory contrasts are tested with Holm’s step-down procedure. The design and achieved MDD are printed beside the verdict, and Tango’s paired score interval sits beside it as a cross-check that does not enter the verdict.

A report with a registration, or with confirmatory = TRUE, is evidence, so any row from the dev, exploratory or calibration split is refused with class hr_dev_not_evidence, and so is a registration edited after it was made.

Judges

Some answers cannot be scored by matching text: a summary, an explanation, an answer that is right in other words. hr_judge() asks a model to choose between candidates ("select"), compare two ("pairwise") or grade one against a reference ("grade"). Candidates are shown under the letters A, B and so on, never their names, and each item is asked in two orders. A verdict that changes with the order, mapped back to the candidate it names, is "unresolved", never a pick. This stand-in always picks whatever is shown first:

first <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) '{"verdict": "A", "reason": "It is first."}')
j <- hr_judge(c(short = "Revenue was 45.2 million.", long = "Revenue was 51.8 million."),
              first, mode = "select", rubric = "Which candidate gives fiscal 2024 revenue?")
j$outcome
#> [1] "unresolved"
j$verdicts[, c("order", "shown", "verdict", "value")]
#>   order      shown verdict value
#> 1     1 short,long       A short
#> 2     2 long,short       A  long

The judge’s requests go through the same check as gr_call(), under the labels judge.<mode>.o<k>, into a trace of the judge’s own. Their cost is in j$judge_cost and never in the trace of the run being judged.

hr_judge_config() holds everything that decides a judge’s answers (model, mode, rubric, the package’s instructions, reply schema, orders, how verdicts are combined, the positive grade) with a hash of it. hr_judge_validate() compares the judge’s decisions with blind human labels for one configuration. It refuses fewer than 50 human-positive or 50 human-negative items, with class hr_judge_too_few_labels, and the minimums cannot be lowered: at 10% prevalence, 100 labels hold 10 positives and a sensitivity interval of about plus or minus 0.3. The judge’s decisions here are simulated as right 90% of the time:

gr_register_model("mock-judge", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4)
cfg <- hr_judge_config("mock-judge", "Does the response give the reference's answer?",
                       mode = "grade")

set.seed(3)
human <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(60, 60))
judged <- ifelse(runif(120) < 0.9, human, !human)
judged[c(5, 70)] <- NA       # unresolved by the judge
v <- hr_judge_validate(cfg, data.frame(judge = judged, human = human), B = 200)
v
#> <hr_judge_validation> config e9b61470aa4b (grade, mock-judge)
#>   items: 120 labelled (60 positive, 60 negative), 2 unresolved, 0 dropped
#>   kappa:       0.850 [0.750, 0.950]
#>   sensitivity: 0.933 [0.841, 0.974], n = 60, half-width 0.067
#>   specificity: 0.917 [0.819, 0.964], n = 60
#>   swap inconsistency: 0.017 [0.005, 0.059], 2 of 120

Items the judge left unresolved count as not called positive, which is how the scorer will count them, so the figures describe the judge as it will be used. Whether they are good enough for your purpose is a decision to make before labelling; the function measures and does not admit. The record is keyed by the configuration’s hash, and hr_judge_valid() says when it no longer holds:

hr_judge_valid(v, cfg)
#> [1] TRUE
hr_judge_valid(v, hr_judge_config("mock-judge", "Is the response right?", mode = "grade"))
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"reason")
#> [1] "the judge configuration changed since validation (rubric)"

hr_scorer_judge() is a benchmark scorer that grades each output against its label with a grade-mode judge. It refuses to be built without a valid record (class hr_judge_unvalidated). An unresolved judgement counts as wrong and a failed one as an error, so an arm’s accuracy cannot rise on the items the judge could not settle, and the judge’s requests stay in the scorer’s own trace, out of the benchmark’s cost columns:

grader_judge <- gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shown <- sub(".*Response to grade:", "", messages[[2]]$content)
  ok <- grepl("45.2 million", shown, fixed = TRUE)
  sprintf('{"verdict": "%s", "reason": "Compared."}', if (ok) "pass" else "fail")
})
judge_scorer <- hr_scorer_judge(cfg, v, grader_judge)
judge_scorer$fn("What was revenue?", "It came to 45.2 million dollars.", "45.2 million")$correct
#> [1] TRUE

A judge’s accuracy figures carry its own errors. hr_judge_ppi() corrects judge-scored accuracy with human labels on a sample, by prediction-powered inference (PPI++ by default). Here a lenient judge passes 30% of wrong answers on 1000 items, and people label 150 of them:

set.seed(7)
truth <- rbinom(1000, 1, 0.6)
lenient <- ifelse(truth == 1, rbinom(1000, 1, 0.95), rbinom(1000, 1, 0.3))
labelled <- rep(NA, 1000)
picked <- sample(1000, 150)
labelled[picked] <- truth[picked]
hr_judge_ppi(lenient, labelled)[, c("estimate", "lower", "upper", "judge_mean")]
#>    estimate     lower     upper judge_mean
#> 1 0.5668593 0.5053991 0.6283196      0.698
mean(truth)
#> [1] 0.594

The judge alone says 0.698. Corrected with the 150 labels the estimate is 0.567, and its interval, 0.505 to 0.628, holds the true share of 0.594. When the labelled items were drawn with unequal probabilities, pass inclusion_prob and the correction is inverse probability weighted. The interval is a normal approximation and runs narrow with few labels at small inclusion probabilities.

Baselines without a model

A configuration that calls a model should beat one that does not. hr_baseline_classifier() fits a ridge logistic regression on tf-idf features (hr_tfidf()) and cross-fits it, so every item is predicted by a model that never saw it, with the vocabulary fitted on each training fold only. Folds are stratified by label, or keep each cluster whole:

set.seed(1)
words <- function(pool, n) vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) paste(sample(pool, 6, TRUE), collapse = " "), "")
abstracts <- c(words(c("masks", "infection", "trial", "ward", "virus"), 10),
               words(c("budget", "policy", "school", "survey", "income"), 50))
relevant <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(10, 50))

hr_baseline_classifier(abstracts, relevant, folds = 5)
#> <hr_baseline_classifier> ridge logistic, 2 labels, 5 folds
#>   accuracy: 1.000 [0.940, 1.000], 60 of 60 out of fold
#>   training size per fold: 48, 48, 48, 48, 48

Real abstracts do not separate this cleanly. Run the baseline on the same labelled set as the model screener: a screener no more accurate than it costs calls and buys nothing.

hr_baseline_ranker() simulates prioritised screening over a set whose relevance is known, as ASReview’s simulation mode does: it starts from one relevant and one irrelevant record, refits after each batch, and screens the record with the highest predicted relevance next. It reports the records screened to reach 95% recall and WSS@95, the share left unread at that recall less the 5% a random order would leave:

ranked <- hr_baseline_ranker(abstracts, relevant)
ranked
#> <hr_baseline_ranker> logistic, 60 records, 10 relevant, 9 fits
#>   95% recall after 11 records (random order: 55.5 expected)
#>   WSS@95: 0.767

gr_stop_test() takes this result, or any screening order, and says when prioritised screening may stop; vignette("review") covers it.

Drift

A provider can change a model behind the same name. hr_drift_check() reruns an arm live on the items of a frozen benchmark and compares the two item by item, with alpha and an optional alert fixed in the call before anything is rerun. Here the model has since learned two capitals wrong:

six <- hr_reference(
  items = list(q1 = "France", q2 = "Peru", q3 = "Chad", q4 = "Fiji", q5 = "Chile", q6 = "Laos"),
  labels = c("Paris", "Lima", "N'Djamena", "Suva", "Santiago", "Vientiane"),
  cluster = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c", "c"), split = "test")
then <- c(France = "Paris", Peru = "Lima", Chad = "N'Djamena", Fiji = "Suva",
          Chile = "Santiago", Laos = "Vientiane")
now <- then
now[c("Chad", "Laos")] <- c("Ndjamena", "Luang Prabang")
answers <- function(table) {
  gr_mock_client(function(messages, params) table[[sub("Capital of ", "", messages[[1]]$content)]])
}

frozen <- hr_benchmark(capital, six, runs = 5, client = answers(then))
drift <- hr_drift_check(frozen, capital, client = answers(now), reference = six,
                        alert = 0.1, B = 500)
drift
#> <hr_drift_check> arm 'capital': 5 frozen run(s) vs 5 live, 6 item(s) in 3 cluster(s); alpha 0.05
#> (a) Accuracy: frozen 1.000, live 0.667, change -0.333 [-0.500, -0.167], p 0.0122; changed: yes
#>     Clustered McNemar (Obuchowski): X^2 4.000, p 0.0455; agrees: yes
#> (b) Flips: between frozen runs 0.000, between live runs 0.000, frozen vs live 0.333, excess 0.333 (one-sided lower 0.000), p 0.333; in excess: no
#>     Frozen pairs flip 0.000 to 0.000; frozen-live pairs 0.333 to 0.333
#> Drift: yes; alert at 0.100: crossed
#> Items: lost 2, gained 0, worse 0, better 0, same 4 
#>  item cluster change frozen live  frozen_outcome live_outcome 
#>  q3   b       lost   1.000  0.000 n'djamena      ndjamena     
#>  q6   c       lost   1.000  0.000 vientiane      luang prabang
#> Note: 6 items in 3 clusters fall short of 300 items and 30 clusters, where the cluster bootstrap can undercover; read the tests as approximate.

Test (a) is the change in accuracy, live minus frozen, by a cluster bootstrap over documents, with the clustered McNemar test beside it. Test (b) asks whether frozen and live runs disagree more than replicate runs disagree among themselves; per item it estimates the squared change, so it also sees losses and gains that cancel in accuracy. Here (a) finds the two lost items, a change of -0.333 with an interval that lies wholly beyond the alert of 0.1. Test (b) does not reject: with three clusters its one-sided bound reaches 0. The live rerun is in drift$live, an hr_bench you can report or keep as the next frozen sample. Fewer than 5 frozen runs, a changed arm, another reference or scorer, and a live rerun answered from a cache or a recording are refused: that last one would be the frozen reply again, not the model today.

Signals, calibration and gate thresholds

Some readers report on their own work: the iterative reader says at each step whether it can answer, preview says which sections its plan would skip, and ensemble says how it settled its members. hr_signal() records such a value as a local step in the trace, which sends no request and changes no cache key, and hr_signals() reads them back:

reader <- gr_mock_client(function(m, p) {
  '{"can_answer": true, "answer": "45.2 million dollars", "next_query": ""}'
})
ch <- gr_segment(gr_example(), list(method = "sentence", max_tokens = 150))
read <- gr_read(ch, "What was revenue?", reader, "iterative")
hr_signals(read)[, c("signal", "value", "score", "refs")]
#>                    signal value score        refs
#> 1 gr.iterative.can_answer  TRUE     1 {"round":1}

A signal is advisory. Nothing in the package acts on one, and a signal may gate an action only after it has been measured against items whose right answer is known. hr_calibrate_signal() does that on a graded set, which must include unanswerable items: a signal measured only on answerable questions has never been asked about the case where “I can answer” is most often wrong. It fits a map from the signal to a probability on half of each cluster’s items and measures it on the other half, with the Brier score, type-2 AUROC, the area under the risk-coverage curve and a debiased calibration error, each with a cluster bootstrap interval. The record is keyed by the served model, its version, the task, format, prompt hash, effort, module and contract version. The graded set here is simulated, 1200 items in 120 documents:

set.seed(2)
n <- 1200
answerable <- runif(n) < 0.8
score <- runif(n) * ifelse(answerable, 1, 0.6)
graded <- data.frame(cluster = rep(sprintf("doc%03d", 1:120), each = 10),
                     score = score, answerable = answerable,
                     correct = runif(n) < plogis(-6 + 12 * score) / ifelse(answerable, 1, 3))
key <- list(served_model = "mock-large-2026-01", version = "2026-01", task = "qa",
            format = "txt", prompt_hash = "a1b2c3", effort = NA, module = "iterative")

cal <- hr_calibrate_signal("gr.iterative.can_answer", graded, key, seed = 3, B = 200)
cal
#> <hr_calibration> gr.iterative.can_answer: advisory
#>   1200 items (715 wrong, 266 unanswerable) in 120 clusters; map: platt
#>   key: served_model=mock-large-2026-01, version=2026-01, task=qa, format=txt, prompt_hash=a1b2c3, effort=NA, module=iterative, contract_version=0.1
#>   calibration half: 600 items, accuracy 0.400
#>   brier   0.0914  [0.0761, 0.1075]
#>   auroc2  0.9454  [0.9282, 0.9619]
#>   aurc    0.2677  [0.2358, 0.3110]
#>   ece     0.0695  [0.0264, 0.1021]
#>   advisory: no gate threshold has been set

A new record is always advisory. hr_gate_threshold() looks for the loosest threshold at which acting on the items at or above it keeps a risk below alpha with confidence 1 - delta, by Learn-then-Test: thresholds are tested from strict to loose with a one-sided Clopper-Pearson bound, and the sequence stops at the first that fails. Errors from one document go together, so the bound is taken on an effective number of items, n / deff, where the design effect deff is measured over the calibration half’s clusters at each threshold. alpha has no default, since it is a decision about the task:

cal <- hr_gate_threshold(cal, "stop", alpha = 0.1)
as.data.frame(cal$gate[c("threshold", "n", "k", "deff", "ucb", "coverage", "status")])
#>   threshold   n k     deff        ucb coverage status
#> 1 0.8510243 147 7 1.258159 0.09408169    0.245 passed
cal$status
#> [1] "gating"

At the threshold kept, 147 items of the calibration half are acted on, 7 of them wrongly. The design effect is 1.26, so the bound counts them as about 117 independent items, and the upper bound on the error among them is 0.094 (0.088 if the items were independent). A record becomes "gating" only with a passing threshold, at least 100 wrong items in the graded set, a map that rises with the signal and a calibration error over at least 5 bins. Items with the same p share a bin, so a signal with fewer than 5 values, such as a logical one, stays advisory. A graded set with a split column, as hr_assign_splits() gives, is calibrated on its calibration rows alone. Even then the signal gates only through a policy, and only for a run whose key matches the record:

policy <- hr_signal_policy("gr.iterative.can_answer", "stop")
hr_apply_signal(c(0.95, 0.4), policy, cal, key)[, c("value", "p", "gated", "act", "route")]
#>   value         p gated   act       route
#> 1  0.95 0.9938152  TRUE  TRUE         act
#> 2   0.4 0.1982915  TRUE FALSE route_check

later <- utils::modifyList(key, list(served_model = "mock-large-2026-06"))
hr_calibration_valid(cal, later)
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"differs")
#> [1] "served_model"
hr_apply_signal(0.95, policy, cal, later)$reason
#> [1] "the record does not hold for this run (served_model differs)"

When the signal cannot gate, the item is routed by on_fail: to a check (the default), to a person, or nowhere. No reader calls hr_apply_signal() yet, so in this release nothing gates on a signal.

The statistics underneath

The functions above rest on five that can be used on their own.

hr_prop_ci() gives Wilson, Clopper-Pearson or Jeffreys intervals for a proportion. Use Wilson for a descriptive rate and Clopper-Pearson for an “at least” or “at most” claim, read as a one-sided bound:

hr_prop_ci(46, 50)[, c("est", "lower", "upper", "method")]
#>    est     lower     upper method
#> 1 0.92 0.8116175 0.9684505 wilson
hr_prop_ci(46, 50, method = "clopper_pearson", side = "lower")[, c("lower", "method", "side")]
#>       lower          method  side
#> 1 0.8262088 clopper_pearson lower

hr_agreement() reports agreement between two raters as the count table with observed agreement, Cohen’s kappa with a bootstrap interval, the prevalence and bias indices, PABAK, Gwet’s AC1, and sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV when positive is given. Kappa is never reported alone, since it moves with prevalence as much as with agreement. For a matrix of coders, or an ordinal, interval or ratio level, it reports Krippendorff’s alpha instead, and only percent agreement below 30 items.

screener <- rep(c("keep", "drop", "keep", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
person   <- rep(c("keep", "keep", "drop", "drop"), c(40, 9, 6, 45))
hr_agreement(screener, person, positive = "keep", B = 200)$stats[1:4, ]
#>            statistic  estimate        se     lower     upper
#> 1 observed agreement 0.8500000        NA 0.7671644 0.9069401
#> 2              kappa 0.6995192 0.0713936 0.5620888 0.8377657
#> 3              PABAK 0.7000000        NA 0.5343288 0.8138803
#> 4                AC1 0.7007481 0.0713518 0.5591707 0.8423256

hr_ht_estimate() estimates a total, a mean or a ratio from a sample drawn with known inclusion probabilities, optionally by stratum; it is how screening recall is weighted on a stacked reference. hr_ppi() is the prediction-powered estimate behind hr_judge_ppi(). hr_alt_test() runs the alternative annotator test of Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025), which asks whether a model’s labels can stand in for those of three or more people, with the margin set by the people’s declared expertise (expertise has no default):

set.seed(3)
gold <- sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, replace = TRUE)
noisy <- function(p) ifelse(runif(80) < p, gold, sample(c("a", "b", "c"), 80, TRUE))
people <- sapply(1:4, function(j) noisy(0.75))
alt <- hr_alt_test(noisy(0.95), people, expertise = "skilled")
alt$omega
#> [1] 1
alt$passed
#> [1] TRUE

The model here wins against each of the four annotators, so the winning rate omega is 1 and the test passes; it needs at least 30 items with two or more human labels, and warns below 50.
